title: Pulmonary Nodule: Risk-Stratify Before You Chase It
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule is managed by malignancy risk, size, morphology, growth and patient factors—not by reflex biopsy or repeated CT without a plan. Symptoms such as hemoptysis or unexplained weight loss move the patient into diagnostic evaluation rather than routine surveillance.
recognize: Risk rises with smoking exposure, older age, prior cancer, suspicious morphology, upper-lobe location and documented growth.
Many small nodules are benign and require surveillance rather than immediate invasive testing.
differentiate: A nodule in an asymptomatic screening context differs from a lesion found during evaluation of hemoptysis, weight loss or persistent focal symptoms.
Prior granulomatous infection does not automatically prove benignity.
assessment: Review smoking history, prior malignancy, immune status, TB/fungal exposure, symptoms, comorbidity and old imaging.
Compare with the oldest available imaging before calling a lesion new or growing.
workup: Use a validated radiology/nodule pathway for surveillance interval and need for PET-CT, specialty referral or tissue diagnosis.
Avoid serial imaging without a documented endpoint and owner.
management: Follow low-risk lesions using the applicable Canadian/provincial pathway and refer higher-risk or growing lesions to lung-cancer/thoracic expertise.
Symptomatic or clearly suspicious lesions require diagnostic workup rather than routine screening follow-up.
medicationSafety: Consider renal function/contrast allergy only when contrast imaging is actually indicated.
Do not delay cancer workup with repeated empiric infection treatment when a suspicious lesion persists.
counselling: Explain absolute risk and why surveillance can be safer than immediate biopsy.
Support smoking cessation without making cessation a prerequisite for diagnostic care.
followUp: Assign ownership of the next imaging/referral date and close the loop on every recommended study.
examTrap: Biopsying every small incidental nodule—or treating a symptomatic suspicious lesion as merely a screening finding.
oneLinePearl: Nodule care is risk plus growth plus symptoms, with explicit follow-up ownership.
sourceBasis: Canadian lung-nodule and thoracic imaging pathways
Cancer Care Ontario lung pathways where applicable

title: Interstitial Lung Disease: Recognize the Pattern and Refer Early
bottomLine: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, inspiratory crackles and restrictive/diffusion abnormalities should raise ILD concern. Identify medication, occupational, autoimmune and exposure clues, obtain appropriate imaging/PFTs, and refer before progressive fibrosis is mistaken for recurrent infection.
recognize: Bibasal fine inspiratory crackles, clubbing, exertional desaturation and restrictive physiology are important clues.
Connective-tissue disease, birds/mould, drugs and occupational exposures can cause secondary ILD.
differentiate: Heart failure, COPD, infection and pulmonary vascular disease can mimic dyspnea/interstitial abnormalities.
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude early ILD when suspicion remains high.
assessment: Ask tempo, exertional limitation, autoimmune symptoms, smoking, birds/mould, occupation, medications, cancer therapy and family history.
Assess oxygenation at rest and with exertion when appropriate.
workup: Use high-resolution CT and full PFTs when ILD is suspected; use autoimmune/infectious testing when the differential supports it.
Before immunosuppression, follow current Canadian infection-screening guidance.
management: Refer suspected fibrotic/progressive ILD to respirology/ILD expertise and treat the underlying cause where identifiable.
Pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and oxygen assessment are useful adjuncts.
medicationSafety: Antifibrotic and immunosuppressive therapies require diagnosis-specific monitoring and specialty oversight.
Do not start prolonged steroids for an undifferentiated interstitial pattern before important infection is considered.
redFlags: Immunosuppressed patient with new diffuse infiltrates
counselling: Explain why establishing the ILD subtype matters because treatments differ.
Discuss exposure avoidance when a credible driver exists.
followUp: Track symptoms, lung function, oxygen needs and imaging according to specialty guidance.
examTrap: Repeating antibiotics for progressive dry cough and bilateral interstitial change without considering ILD.
oneLinePearl: ILD is a pattern to classify early, not a pneumonia label to recycle.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society ILD guideline/position-statement library

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Confirm the Disorder, Then Make PAP Usable
bottomLine: OSA is diagnosed with an appropriate sleep study in the right clinical context, not from snoring or a questionnaire alone. Treatment succeeds when PAP or another appropriate therapy is indicated, usable and followed for residual sleepiness, leak, pressure/mask problems and driving risk.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, nocturnal choking, resistant hypertension and daytime sleepiness raise probability.
Normal BMI does not exclude OSA.
differentiate: Insomnia, insufficient sleep, circadian disorder, medication effects, depression and central sleep apnea can produce fatigue/sleepiness with different management.
Screening questionnaires estimate probability; they do not establish OSA.
assessment: Assess sleepiness, witnessed events, driving/work risk, sleep duration, alcohol/sedatives, nasal symptoms and cardiometabolic disease.
workup: Choose home testing versus laboratory polysomnography according to comorbidity, pretest probability and local pathway.
Reassess high-risk persistent symptoms after a negative or technically inadequate home study.
management: Use PAP when indicated and troubleshoot mask fit, humidification, nasal obstruction, pressure intolerance and behavioural barriers.
Consider oral appliance, positional or other therapies for selected patients.
medicationSafety: Alcohol, opioids and sedative-hypnotics can worsen sleep-disordered breathing or respiratory risk.
Do not mask untreated OSA with stimulant therapy without reassessing persistent sleepiness.
counselling: Discuss driving safety explicitly when sleepiness is significant.
Frame PAP adherence as a troubleshooting problem rather than failure.
followUp: Review objective PAP use, residual events/leak and symptoms; persistent symptoms require diagnosis/treatment reassessment.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from a high screening score without confirmatory testing—or declaring PAP failure before troubleshooting barriers.
oneLinePearl: Screen for OSA, test for OSA, then make treatment workable.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society / Canadian Sleep Society resources

title: Pleural Effusion: Explain the Fluid Before Repeating the Tap
bottomLine: A pleural effusion is a finding with a cause. Decide whether the pattern fits a known transudative process or requires diagnostic sampling, and escalate infection, respiratory compromise, hemothorax or malignancy concern rather than repeatedly diuresing an unexplained unilateral effusion.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain, decreased breath sounds and dullness are common but nonspecific.
Unilateral, large, recurrent or febrile effusions are more likely to need diagnostic evaluation.
differentiate: Heart failure commonly causes bilateral/transudative effusions, but unilateral or atypical collections deserve broader evaluation.
Parapneumonic/empyema, malignancy, PE and hemothorax change urgency and treatment.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, fever/sepsis, chest pain, malignancy history, heart/liver/renal disease, anticoagulation, trauma and recent procedures.
workup: Use chest imaging/ultrasound to confirm and characterize fluid; select diagnostic thoracentesis based on clinical context.
When sampled, interpret pleural chemistry, cells, microbiology and cytology according to the differential.
management: Treat the cause and drain complicated infection or clinically significant symptomatic collections through the appropriate pathway.
Suspected empyema requires urgent antibiotics plus drainage/source-control planning.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants/bleeding risk before invasive drainage using current procedural guidance.
Avoid repeated diuretic escalation for an unexplained unilateral effusion without reassessment.
counselling: Explain that drainage may be diagnostic, therapeutic or both.
followUp: Close the loop on cytology/culture and recurrent unexplained effusion.
examTrap: Assuming every effusion in heart failure is volume overload despite unilateral recurrence, fever or pleuritic pain.
oneLinePearl: Effusion management starts by asking why the fluid is there.

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize First, Then Find the Source
bottomLine: Hemoptysis ranges from blood-streaked sputum to a life-threatening airway emergency. Distinguish pulmonary bleeding from nasopharyngeal/GI sources, then prioritize airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics and ongoing bleeding before etiologic workup.
recognize: Bronchiectasis, infection, malignancy, PE and airway disease are important causes; anticoagulation can worsen bleeding without explaining the source.
Danger is determined by airway/respiratory compromise and ongoing bleeding, not a memorized volume cutoff alone.
differentiate: Hematemesis is usually GI; posterior epistaxis can mimic hemoptysis.
Minor blood-streaked sputum differs from recurrent hemoptysis in a high-risk smoker.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics, ongoing bleeding, anticoagulants, infection symptoms, cancer/TB risk and PE features.
workup: Use chest imaging and CBC/coagulation studies based on severity/differential; CT/bronchoscopy pathways depend on stability and suspected source.
Use airborne precautions/TB testing when epidemiology and symptoms support it.
management: Unstable or significant ongoing bleeding requires emergency support and urgent respiratory/interventional/thoracic evaluation.
Treat the identified cause; do not stop anticoagulation and discharge without source evaluation when bleeding is significant.
medicationSafety: Review antithrombotics and reversal need according to severity/indication while considering thrombosis risk.
Avoid unnecessary NSAIDs during active clinically important bleeding.
counselling: Give explicit emergency-return instructions for increasing blood, dyspnea, syncope or chest pain.
followUp: Ensure imaging/specialty follow-up is completed even if bleeding stops when malignancy or structural disease remains plausible.
examTrap: Calling hemoptysis 'just anticoagulation' without investigating the pulmonary source.
oneLinePearl: In hemoptysis, protect the airway and explain the bleeding source.
sourceBasis: Canadian Tuberculosis Standards where TB is plausible

title: Chronic Cough: Work the Algorithm, Not the Antibiotic Refill
bottomLine: Chronic cough needs structured history, medication/exposure review and targeted testing. Upper-airway disease, asthma/eosinophilic airway disease and reflux are common, but hemoptysis, weight loss, abnormal imaging, TB risk, ACE-inhibitor exposure and smoking-related disease change the pathway.
recognize: Cough timing, triggers, sputum and associated upper-airway/reflux/asthma symptoms narrow the differential.
ACE inhibitors can cause chronic cough even after prior tolerance.
differentiate: Do not diagnose GERD solely because cough is unexplained; empiric trials need a plausible syndrome and reassessment point.
Abnormal imaging, hemoptysis or systemic symptoms require diagnostic escalation.
assessment: Review smoking/vaping, ACE inhibitor, occupation, nasal symptoms, wheeze, reflux, dysphagia/aspiration, TB risk and red flags.
workup: Use chest radiography and spirometry when appropriate, followed by cause-directed testing.
Avoid serial antibiotics without evidence of bacterial disease.
management: Remove a likely medication cause when appropriate, treat confirmed upper-airway/asthma/reflux disease and reassess response.
Refer refractory/unexplained cough or abnormal imaging as indicated.
medicationSafety: Chronic opioid cough suppression adds sedation/dependence risk and can mask progression.
Do not escalate inhaled corticosteroid indefinitely without phenotype or response evidence.
counselling: Explain that chronic cough often requires sequential hypothesis testing with defined stop/review points.
followUp: Document response to each intervention and reconsider the diagnosis when expected response does not occur.
examTrap: Giving repeated antibiotics to chronic cough without reassessing medications, asthma or imaging.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is an algorithm, not an antibiotic refill diagnosis.

title: Tuberculosis: Infection, Disease, and Public-Health Action Are Different
bottomLine: A positive TST or IGRA indicates TB infection risk, not active TB disease. Before preventive therapy, exclude active disease; when pulmonary TB is plausible, use appropriate isolation/public-health pathways and obtain microbiologic testing rather than starting latent-TB treatment blindly.
recognize: Persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis and epidemiologic risk raise concern for active pulmonary TB.
Latent TB infection is asymptomatic and noninfectious but carries future progression risk.
differentiate: TST/IGRA cannot distinguish latent infection from active disease.
BCG affects TST interpretation more than IGRA; test choice depends on age/context and Canadian standards.
assessment: Assess symptoms, prior TB/treatment, residence/travel in high-incidence regions, exposures, immune suppression, pregnancy and medication interactions.
workup: For suspected active pulmonary TB obtain chest imaging and respiratory specimens for molecular testing, smear/culture and susceptibility per Canadian standards.
Use TST/IGRA for infection screening only when there is a clinical/public-health indication and a plan to act.
management: Notify/coordinate with public health as required and use airborne precautions for suspected infectious pulmonary TB.
Treat TB disease/preventive therapy using current Canadian Tuberculosis Standards rather than memorized legacy regimens.
medicationSafety: TB regimens have major hepatic, interaction, ocular and adherence-monitoring considerations.
Do not give single-drug latent-TB therapy to someone with unrecognized active disease.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and explain infection versus contagious disease.
Discuss adherence, interactions and public-health follow-up clearly.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/susceptibilities, public-health actions and preventive-treatment completion.
examTrap: Starting latent-TB treatment after a positive IGRA without first assessing for active disease.
oneLinePearl: A positive TB infection test starts classification; it does not diagnose active disease.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada TB resources

title: Lung Cancer Screening: High-Risk Screening Is Not Symptom Workup
bottomLine: Low-dose CT lung-cancer screening is for asymptomatic people who meet a current organized-program high-risk pathway. Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, suspicious imaging or persistent focal symptoms require diagnostic evaluation instead of waiting for screening.
recognize: Eligibility varies by province/territory and can use organized risk-assessment models rather than one universal Canada-wide age/pack-year rule.
Screening findings require structured follow-up; the screening CT is not the endpoint.
differentiate: Screening means asymptomatic high-risk testing; symptoms or a concerning known finding require a diagnostic pathway.
Smoking-cessation treatment should be offered whether or not screening eligibility is met.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then smoking exposure, prior cancer, comorbidity, treatment candidacy and local screening access.
workup: Use the current provincial/territorial organized screening pathway; Ontario uses the Ontario Lung Screening Program risk assessment.
Use diagnostic imaging/workup rather than screening referral when symptoms are present.
management: Refer eligible asymptomatic high-risk patients to the organized program and ensure abnormal findings complete recommended follow-up.
Offer evidence-based smoking-cessation treatment without making cessation a condition of care.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric antibiotic/steroid trials that delay evaluation of suspicious lesions or symptom patterns.
Contrast/renal considerations apply only when downstream diagnostic imaging uses contrast; screening LDCT is generally noncontrast.
counselling: Discuss potential benefit, false positives, incidental findings and downstream procedures.
Explain screening is not a substitute for symptom evaluation.
followUp: Track every abnormal screen until its imaging/diagnostic endpoint is completed.
examTrap: Sending new hemoptysis into a routine screening pathway instead of diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; symptoms mean diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario Ontario Lung Screening Program
